latest_report_detail.epidemiological_comments: A total of 2,500 koi fish were being cultured in a tourist pond located in Xinpi Township, Pingtung county. An unexpected mortality event occurred on December 6, 2025, resulting in the death of 330 koi fish over the following two days. On December 8, 2025, the Local Animal Disease Inspection Authority (LADIA) collected two fish and intact samples, and sent them to the National Reference Laboratory (Veterinary Research Institute) for diagnosis. The remaining fish were restricted and disinfectants have been provided to sanitise the surrounding areas of the pond. The PCR results indicated positive reactions to the nucleic acid of Koi herpesvirus (KHV) on December 18, 2025. As of March 16, 2026, no other cases of the same or simillar diseases have been reported in tourist ponds elsewhere in Chinese Taipei.

latest_report_detail.epidemiological_comments: The outbreak, with clinical symptoms and mortality, was contained to one biosecurity unit of Red abalone (Haliotis rufescens) broodstock animals. All animals in the affected unit (120 animals) were culled immediately after confirmation. The farm consists of Red abalone (H. rufescens), Japanese abalone (Haliotis discus hannai) and Hybrid red × Japanese abalone (H. rufescens × H. discus hannai) across broodstock/spawning, hatchery, nursery and grow‑out units. Although Japanese Abalone and hybrids are physically separated and strict biosecurity applies between units, they form part of the overall epidemiological system and have not yet been screened for Withering Syndrome. Progeny originating from the affected broodstock may be present in other units; the disease status of these units is currently unknown. A full epidemiological investigation is ongoing, and screening of all units on the farm is being initiated. Until this process is completed, the event remains classified as continuing.

latest_report_detail.epidemiological_comments: Wild school prawn (Metapenaeus macleayi) samples have tested positive for white spot syndrome virus by real-time, conventional PCR and sequencing of the amplicons. Samples were collected from sites within the existing movement control zones in northern NSW. Testing was undertaken as part of a routine surveillance program and no clinical signs were observed in the WSSV-positive animals. Whole genome sequencing and analysis indicates that the strain of WSSV is the same as the strain from other detections in northern NSW. A control zone covering these areas is in place to prevent spread of WSSV from the zone. This event is epidemiologically linked to event 4586. The detection reported in this immediate notification occurred within the control zone that was established based on the outbreaks reported in event 4586. It occurred in the framework of targeted surveillance attempted to demonstrate a zone freedom.

latest_report_detail.epidemiological_comments: Tilapia lake virus (TiLV) was last reported in 2017, and no detections have been made since then through active or passive surveillance. The current case was identified through passive surveillance. Affected fish exhibited clinical signs including skin erosion and exophthalmia (ruptured eyes). PCR testing of a dead specimen confirmed the presence of TiLV. Immediate control measures implemented included early harvest, pond drying, and disinfection of ponds and farming equipment. The farmer was advised to strengthen biosecurity practices and to restock with TiLV-negative seed in the next production cycle.

latest_report_detail.epidemiological_comments: This is the first occurrence of Yellow Head Virus genotype 1 (YHV-1) in Malaysia. The infection was detected in Penaeus monodon cultured in ponds located in Selangor, specifically in the districts of Sabak Bernam and Kuala Selangor. The two locations are not epidemiologically linked; however, investigations are ongoing to determine any possible connection. The affected specimens were found dead and exhibited typical clinical signs of cephalothorax yellowing. Immediate control measures implemented included early harvest, pond drying, and disinfection of ponds and farming equipment. Farmers were advised to strengthen biosecurity practices and to restock with YHV-1–free seed in the next production cycle.

latest_report_detail.epidemiological_comments: 20,000 tails of Grouper (Honeycomb Grouper x Giant Grouper) (Epinephelus merra x Epinephelus lanceolatus) were imported from Chinese Taipei in early July 2024 onto a fish farm. Fish mortalities were found with no significant clinical signs with onset mid-Jul 2024. About 16,000 tails (80%) of fish were lost in the outbreak. No lesions were observed by the fish farmer. Samples were submitted for PCR testing in late July 2024 and the spleen and kidney samples tested positive in red sea bream iridovirus genome detection. Control measures were taken including temporary withholding of feed and increased aeration. No further outbreak was detected. The outbreak and event was considered resolved.

latest_report_detail.epidemiological_comments: Infectious spleen and kidney necrosis virus (ISKNV) was detected in a group of imported cockatoo dwarf cichlid fish (Apistogramma cacatuoides). All the affected fish were depopulated and tanks cleaned and disinfected. No affected fish were shipped from the site. An epidemiologic investigation has indicated minimal risk of exposure to free-living wild or farmed susceptible fish species. ISKNV has historically been sporadically detected in ornamental fish and cultured tilapia populations in the United States. This report documents the first detection of ISKNV in the United States since Megalocytivirus pagrus 1 was added to the WOAH list of aquatic animal diseases.

latest_report_detail.epidemiological_comments: Perkinsus olseni was detected in an imported ornamental captive wild boring clam (Tridacna crocea). Affected and exposed imported animals were confined in a closed aquarium facility with effluent water treatment procedures in place from the time of their arrival. No susceptible animals have moved off of the affected premises. There is no known exposure to other domestic wild or farmed mollusk populations. Depopulation was completed on 4/4/2024, disposal was completed on 4/5/2024. Adult manila clams (Ruditapes philippinarum) were placed in enclosure sourced water as sentinel mollusks to monitor for possible recurrence of Perkinsus olseni. Sentinel mollusks were collected and sampled on 7 Nov 2024 and 3 Dec 2024. Perkinsus olseni was not detected in all samples by histopathology or polymerase chain reaction (PCR).

latest_report_detail.epidemiological_comments: White spot disease was detected in black tiger prawns (Penaeus monodon) in 3 farms in NSW. • Genomic analysis of the WSSV strains detected on the affected farms in northern NSW shows they are identical to each other, and similar to the WSSV strain detected in an enclosed prawn facility in the same area in August 2022, suggesting the two events are linked. They are a different lineage to the Queensland WSSV strain detected in 2016–2020. Investigations have not been able to determine the origin of the infection. Surveillance in and around the affected zone commenced in October 2023, following completion of decontamination and disinfection activities on all affected farms.

latest_report_detail.epidemiological_comments: 1.8 million clams were cultured in a clam farm located in Fangyuan Township, Changhua County. However, an unexpected and consecutive clam mortality event occurred starting in early April 2023. On June 1, the Local Animal Disease Inspection Authority (LADIA) collected six samples from weakened clams and sent them to the National Reference Laboratory (Veterinary Research Institute, formerly named as Animal Health Reach Institute ) for diagnosis. The RT-PCR results indicated positive reactions to the nucleic acid of Perkinsus olseni on July 11. Furthermore, despite the absence of significant gross lesions, immature Perkinsus olseni (trophozoites) were observed during histological examination. By July 7, a total of 90,000 clams were dead and considered to be caused by a co-infection of Perkinsus olseni and bacterial infection (Vibrio spp.). The remaining clams were harvested on August 1. As of September 14, 2023, no other cases of the same or similar diseases have been reported in clam farms elsewhere in Chinese Taipei.

latest_report_detail.epidemiological_comments: 3,000 frogs were kept in a fish farm in Chaozhou Township, Pingtung County, but they had been dying unexpectedly in succession since April 11th, 2023. Thus, the owner reported to the Local Animal Disease Inspection Authority (LADIA) on April 21st. LADIA took three samples of frozen frogs and organs and sent them to the National Reference Laboratory (Animal Health Research Institute) for diagnosis. Meanwhile, the farm owner thoroughly cleaned and disinfected the frog farm. For the frog farm case, the RT-PCR result showed positive reactions to the nucleic acid of ranavirus on May 5th. According to the owner, in May, no abnormal mortality in the frog farm was observed, and he estimated death cases of frogs were 1,500. Therefore, the 50% mortality observed from the frog farm was considered to be caused by co-infection of ranavirus and bacterial (Aeromonas spp.) infection. In Taiwan, no other cases of the same or similar diseases were reported from other frog farms as of July 25th, 2023.

latest_report_detail.epidemiological_comments: A total of 8,000 fish were kept on a fish farm in the Tucheng District of New Taipei City. Fish on the farm have died unexpectedly in succession since September 14, 2022. Subsequently, the fish farm owner reported the situation to the Local Animal Disease Inspection Authority (LADIA) on September 21. The LADIA took two samples of frozen fish and sent them to the National Reference Laboratory (Animal Health Research Institute) for diagnosis. In addition, the fish farm owner thoroughly cleaned and disinfected the surrounding area in the fish farm on September 22. For the fish farm case, the RT-PCR result showed positive reactions to the nucleic acid of tilapia lake virus (TiLV) on September 30. According to the fish farm owner, as of October 5, no abnormal mortality of the fish farm was observed, and the number of estimated death cases of fish was 500. The 6.25% mortality observed from the fish farm was considered to be caused by co-infection of the TiLV and bacterial (Francisella sp.) infection. No other cases of the same or similar diseases have been reported from other fish farms in Taiwan, as of January 5, 2023.

latest_report_detail.disease_name: Infectious salmon anaemia virus (Inf. with) (HPR-deleted or HPR0 genotypes)
latest_report_detail.epidemiological_comments: --Update 18 Aug 2022--Maine (ME): Harvest of the affected site was completed on 4 August 2022. Surveillance sampling and testing continued through the harvest and there were no additional ISAV detections. --Maine (ME): As part of routine monthly surveillance, North American HPR-deleted infectious salmon anemia virus (ISAV) was confirmed in tissues from three farmed Atlantic salmon collected from 2 cages at the same marine site. The samples were collected under the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) Animal Plant Health Inspection Services (APHIS) Veterinary Services (VS) ISAV Control Program in Maine. Amplicon sequencing (segment 6 HPR and segment 8) confirmed North American HPR-deleted ISAV. There were no clinical signs of disease observed and no increased mortality. The affected cages have been harvested. Enhanced surveillance of the remaining 18 cages is occurring and they will be harvested out over the next month. The last US detection of North American HPR-deleted ISAV in farmed Atlantic salmon was in 2006.

latest_report_detail.epidemiological_comments: 17th February: An on-land farm introduced juveniles of whiteleg shrimp (Litopenaeus vannamei) that were imported from Thailand. The prefectural government demanded the farm to inspect the shrimps for six months from the introduction day because they were imported live shrimp juveniles. 23rd - 24th February: Mass mortality events of whiteleg shrimp juveniles occurred. 24thFebruary: The prefectural experimental station conducted field survey at the farm and PCR test for several pathogens in shrimp. As a result ofnested PCR, acute hepatopancreatic necrosis disease (AHND) was suspected on 25th February. 26th February - 2nd March: Fisheries Technology Institute, which is in charge of confirmatory diagnosis in aquatic animals, confirmed positive for AHND by nested PCR and sequencing of the PCR product. Said farm is on-land farm with recirculation filtration system (the rearing water is not drained outside the farm). All the imported shrimp juveniles had been kept in the farm and nojuvenile has been distributed to another place since the introduction into the farm. Important: This immediate notification, initially received by mail by the OIE on 4th March 2021 during the transition period between WAHIS and OIE-WAHIS, was recreated in the new system once it went live. However, OIE-WAHIS prevents the use of a date of report different from the date of submission, hence the date of report being different to its actual date of submission to the OIE.

latest_report_detail.epidemiological_comments: Clinical ISAV outbreak in one sea cage out of 11 at the farming site. Samples were investigated at the National Reference Laboratory by real-time qPCR, with positive outcome. The virus samples were sent to the laboratory Genewiz in Leipzig (Germany) for further examination by sequencing for final confirmation. The fish in the affected cage was immediately killed and destroyed. The rest of the farm site is under official movement restrictions and strict health surveillance (general clinical surveillance and regular sampling). Follow up report 17.12.2021: Sanitary slaughter from the remaining ten cages at the farming site has been initiated. The plan is to complete the slaughtering by the end of January 2022. Follow up report 8.2.2022: All fish from the infected sea cages has been killed and emergency harvest has been carried out in the remaining sea cages at the farming site. All sanitary measures have been carried out and restrictions lifted, but the neighboring farming sites remain under close surveillance.

latest_report_detail.causal_agent: Infectious spleen and kidney necrosis virus (ISKNV)
latest_report_detail.epidemiological_comments: Since the immediate notification sent in February 2021, the official veterinary service has been conducting investigations in fish farms in the provinces of Goiás, Tocantins, Minas Gerais, São Paulo, Mato Grosso do Sul, Paraná, Bahia and Distrito Federal, with samples collected in 23 farms and the detection, up to October 2021, of 11 other outbreaks in dams in Goiás, São Paulo, Minas Gerais, Mato Grosso do Sul and Bahia. Epidemiological and health data were analysed for all farms under passive or active surveillance. The investigations and their analysis allowed options for monitoring on-going disease outbreaks, comparing the disease epidemiology and the different types of fish farming. The official veterinary service continues to carry out epidemiological investigations to understand the animal health situation and to establish, together with the production sector, good practice and biosecurity procedures for the protection of the national aquaculture and fauna, mainly with breeding and fattening farms. No significant morbidity or mortality in ichthyofauna has been observed so far.

latest_report_detail.epidemiological_comments: - Four hundred thousand 30-70 days old bullfrogs were raised on the outbreak farm with 20 ponds in Yanpu Township, Pingtung County. Since June 4, these frogs have developed clinical symptoms such as neurological symptoms, skin bleeding and peeling, and fluid accumulation in the body cavity. More than 1,000 frogs died each day, and the farm owner reported to the Local Animal Disease Inspection Authority on June 24. The farm owner changed the water more frequently and quarantined the infected frogs to prevent the disease from spreading. The farm was thoroughly cleaned and disinfected. By July 16, no more frogs showed clinical signs. There is no other frog farm in the 3 km radius area of the index farm and no other incidents were observed in the immediate area. As of August 30, no other frog farms reported the disease or similar cases.

latest_report_detail.epidemiological_comments: Ostreid herpesvirus-1 microvariant (OsHV-1 microvariant) was detected in sentinel juvenile Pacific oysters, C. gigas, in San Diego Bay, CA. The sentinel animals were sourced from an OsHV-1 tested negative population and deployed at this site as part of a research effort. The affected sentinel population has been depopulated. No commercially farm-raised animals, at any facilities in the U.S., were exposed or affected. The identical OsHV-1 microvariant was first detected in oysters at the same site in San Diego Bay in October 2018. Due to limitations with the WAHIS system, the population of animals is noted to be “farmed”, however, the affected population is more accurately defined as research sentinel animals with exposure to the local environment, not produced for commercial use.

latest_report_detail.epidemiological_comments: White spot syndrome virus (WSSV) has been detected in samples of wild crustaceans from two sites within the WSSV movement restriction area (MRA) in south east Queensland. The detections of WSSV were made during routine six-monthly surveillance. Samples collected from these two sites had last tested positive for WSSV in March 2018. Samples of prawns from two prawn farms located adjacent to the Logan River and also within the MRA have returned positive test results for WSSV. These farms were at the end of their production cycle and both farms are now destocked. Enhanced biosecurity measures are in place and planning for decontamination of the ponds is underway. This is the first detection of WSSV in prawn farms within the MRA since production resumed in 2018 following a WSSV outbreak in 2016. Restrictions on movement of crustaceans, fishing restrictions, biosecurity controls, and surveillance have been in place for the MRA since 16 March 2017 following the first detections of WSSV in the area in wild crustaceans. WSSV has not been detected in any area of Australia outside of the MRA despite a national surveillance program that has been ongoing for more than 2 years. Basic biosecurity conditions for infection with WSSV were reviewed following the 2016 outbreak in south east Queensland and have been in place continuously.

latest_report_detail.epidemiological_comments: Stirlingshire- All effluents were treated and final discharge was collected and also treated. The animals were culled on 16 July 2019, immediately after suspicion of IHHNV and the site has been disinfected.The case can be closed. Lincolnshire site - The final phase of the stock clearance and site disinfection was carried out on the 18th December under supervision of the Competent Authority, completing the three part staged clearance and disinfection of the premises. Further to this restocking has begun with SPF post larval shrimp certified as free from IHHNV. Each consignment has been inspected and sampled on arrival by the Competent Authority with 150 animals collected from each and tested by PCR for IHHNV according to OIE methods, all tests were confirmed as negative for IHHNV. The outbreak can now be closed.

latest_report_detail.epidemiological_comments: The USDA APHIS National Veterinary Services Laboratories (NVSL) confirmed red sea bream iridovirus (RSIV) in imported ornamental fish (common clownfish or Amphirprion ocellaris) that were confined to an aquarium. The clownfish started showing clinical signs of disease during the quarantine period after arrival at the aquarium. Lionfish (Pterosis volitans) that shared the same water at the aquarium with the imported clownfish were also found to be infected with RSIV. The infected fish were never released and were always under containment until euthanized.

latest_report_detail.epidemiological_comments: Des mortalités de Penaeus monodon d’élevage ont été observées dans certains bassins de plusieurs élevages. Un événement de fin 2015 ne répondait pas aux critères de notification immédiate, mais un événement de janvier 2016 y répondait ; par conséquent, les deux événements sont notifiés dans ce rapport. Les animaux étaient atteints 35 à 95 jours après leur introduction. Les taux de mortalité allaient de négligeable à environ 90%. Une hépatopancréatite a été associée aux populations de crevettes atteintes. L’histopathologie des hépatopancréas des animaux atteints était conforme à celle décrite pour la maladie de nécrose hépatopancréatique aiguë ; cependant, la maladie ne répond pas à la définition de cas de cette maladie fournie dans le projet de chapitre du Manuel aquatique de l’OIE distribué aux Membres. Les informations actuelles sur le diagnostic de la maladie figurent ci-dessous : - Un membre du clade Vibrio harveyi a été isolé chez les crevettes atteintes. Vibrio parahaemolyticus a été exclu. - Les PCR (tests AP3 et AP4) des isolats bactériens provenant de crevettes atteintes ont été positives pour les gènes de toxines PirA et PirB. Les tests AP1 et AP2 étaient négatifs (positifs pour les échantillons de contrôle de la maladie de nécrose hépatopancréatique aiguë en provenance d’Asie), indiquant l’absence du plasmide pVA1 associé à la maladie de nécrose hépatopancréatique aiguë. - L’analyse préliminaire de la séquence complète du génome indique que les gènes de toxines PirA et PirB peuvent être intégrés dans le génome de l’isolat bactérien. Les épreuves de laboratoire se poursuivent afin de compléter l’analyse de la séquence complète du génome et d’identifier l’isolat bactérien. Des épreuves biologiques sont envisagées afin de confirmer la pathogénicité de l’isolat. Une enquête nationale sera menée pour déterminer la distribution de la maladie.

latest_report_detail.epidemiological_comments: River Lorrha – Genotyping has indicated that this isolate is Genotype A. Live crayfish were still present on the upper part of the Lorrha. No crayfish were found in other streams that flowed into the east side of Lough Derg. The reasons for these negative results need to be investigated further. Molecular testing of crayfish samples collected were negative for A. astaci which may suggest spread has ceased. River Barrow – Genotyping has indicated that this isolate is Genotype D. Twelve sites were surveyed on the Barrow and live crayfish were found on the Lower Barrow at Graiguenamanagh, the Fushoge and Lerr tributaries, as well as at all sample points upstream of Tankardstown.

latest_report_detail.epidemiological_comments: The USDA Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS) and Texas Parks and Wildlife Department (TPWD) conducted a comprehensive epidemiological investigation and worked collaboratively to respond to the event. A summary of the epidemiological investigation and response is as follows: • The farm was placed under quarantine and all animals have been harvested. • Completed the cleaning and disinfection of the infected premises (including, but not limited to all harvesting equipment, as well as aerators, pumps, and lined nursery pods). In addition, all farm ponds and ditches have been dried and disinfected. • Environmental samples and surveillance in the control area has been negative for AHPND. • As a precaution, additional surveillance and requirements prior to restocking will be carried out by TWPD through the Texas Shrimp Inspection Program. The APHND event is considered closed.

latest_report_detail.epidemiological_comments: An unexplained daily mortality of tilapia fingerlings was observed in the nursery pond of a private farm after stocking on May 16, 2017. Elevated mortality after 15 days reached approximately 25%. Affected fish showed distended abdomen and bulging of the eyes. On May 31, 2017 samples were collected and submitted at the Fisheries Biotechnology Center (FBC) Muñoz, Nueva Ecija. Semi-nested RT-PCR exhibited positive results using reported Tilapia Lake Virus (TiLV) primers. Other samples submitted to National Fisheries Laboratory- Fish Health of the Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources also showed positive results by insulated isothermal PCR (iiPCR). The amplified segment 3 of the viral gene has 94-95% nucleotide similarity to Israel TiLV strain. The movement of fingerlings from the affected pond is restricted and monitored. Results of the last two samplings showed negative for TiLV using iiPCR.

latest_report_detail.epidemiological_comments: Surveillance within 5 km radius around the first infected farm that Chinese Taipei reported to the OIE on 12 June 2017 has been completed. There are totally 46 tilapia farms in the surveillance area which covered all related drainage systems. Samples from all these farms were tested by the National Reference Laboratory, Animal Health Research Institute (AHRI), and 8 out of the 46 farms were confirmed to be positive to tilapia lake virus (TiLV). These infected farms were placed under movement restriction for 2 weeks. However, no abnormal mortality has been observed. The 6.4% mortality observed from the first TiLV infected farm was considered to be caused by secondary bacterial (Francisella-like bacteria) infection.

latest_report_detail.epidemiological_comments: Bonamia ostreae was detected for the first time in New Zealand flat oysters (Ostrea chilensis) in January 2015 on one land based aquaculture facility and on two marine farms in the northern part of the South Island. Since that time, movement controls have been in place to regulate the movement of susceptible shellfish from the upper South Island and active surveillance has been conducted to enhance early detection of spread. In 2016 surveillance detected B. ostreae in the domestic and wild oysters within the same area as initially reported. In May 2017 surveillance detected B. ostreae in a further marine flat oyster farm in Big Glory Bay, Stewart Island (situated at the southern end of the South Island of New Zealand). Movement controls are in place while the long term management options for this range extension are being considered. To date, no clinical signs or elevated mortality has been observed associated with the detections in Big Glory Bay and in wild oysters in the Marlborough Sounds.

latest_report_detail.epidemiological_comments: During 2014 the virus was detected in about ten farms. This virus associated disease was not diagnosed in its clinical form at the Norwegian Veterinary Institute during 2015. The Norwegian Food Safety Authority (NFSA) has established a risk based surveillance program for virus Y. About 65 farms were investigated in 2015 and the infection with the virus Y was detected in nine farms. In six of these farms, the virus had not been detected earlier. The sites positive for virus Y were, however, located in areas where the virus previously had been detected. Neither the disease nor the virus has been detected in Norwegian farmed Atlantic salmon. The NFSA will continue the surveillance program to investigate the prevalence of virus Y in rainbow trout and salmon in areas where the virus previously has been detected. Assessments based on surveillance data and further information of the virus and the disease the NFSA will decide whether to put the virus Y on the national list (List 3).

latest_report_detail.epidemiological_comments: Specimens of Ostrea angasi were examined by histopathology following low level mortalities in trial farming of this oyster species. Histopathology indicated the presence of Bonamia parasites. Subsequent diagnostic tests to confirm Bonamia infection and identify the species are included: Bonamia genus-specific TaqMan qPCR (Corbeil et al. 2006a): positive. OIE Bonamia genus-specific conventional PCR (Cochennec et al. 2000): positive, sequence homology with B. exitiosa. Bonamia ostreae PCR (Ramilo et al. 2013): negative. Bonamia exitiosa PCR (Ramilio et al. 2013): positive, sequence homology with B. exitiosa. Bonamia sp. 18S SSU (571-641) PCR (Corbeil et al. 2006b): positive, sequence homology with B. exitiosa. Haplosporidia sp. PCR (Carnegie et al. 2014): positive, sequence homology with B. exitiosa. ISH Bonamia genus-specific method (Ramilo et al. 2014): positive. The test results from April 2015 did not satisfy the OIE definition of confirmed case of Bonamia exitiosa. Further diagnostic tests were performed and these took considerable time.

latest_report_detail.epidemiological_comments: An investigation into scallop health in the Marlborough Sounds performed by the Ministry for Primary Industries identified an incidental finding of the protozoan parasite Perkinsus olseni in New Zealand Scallops (Pecten Novaezealandiae). The notification is based on New Zealand’s national Animal Health Laboratory verifying the presence of Perkinsus by histopathology and confirming P. olseni via conventional PCR and sequencing. This is the first detection of Perkinsus olseni in New Zealand Scallops (Pecten Novaezealandiae). Perkinsus olseni is known to occur in wild populations of the bivalves Austrovenus stutchburyi (Veneridae), Macomona liliana (Tellinidae), Barbatia novaezealandiae (Arcidae), and Paphies australis (Mesodesmatidae), as well as farmed and wild populations of Haliotis iris (Haliotidae) and has recently been found in a farmed population of Green Lipped Mussels (Perna Canaliculis) in New Zealand. The Animal Health Laboratory has confirmed that this identification of Pecten Novaezealandiae as a susceptible species is in line with chapter 1.5 of the OIE Aquatic Animal Health Code which describes the criteria for listing species as susceptible to a specific pathogen.

latest_report_detail.epidemiological_comments: An aquaculture facility notified the Ministry for Primary Industries of a suspected detection of the protozoan parasite Perkinsus olseni in a New Zealand green lipped mussel (Perna canaliculus). The notification was based on histopathological findings during routine health monitoring by the aquaculture facility. No unusual mortality or signs of ill health have been observed in Perna canaliculus at the facility. New Zealand’s national animal health laboratory verified the presence of Perkinsus by histopathology and confirmed P. olseni via conventional PCR and sequencing. This is the first detection of Perkinsus olseni in New Zealand green lipped mussels. Perkinsus olseni is known to occur in wild populations of the bivalves Austrovenus stutchburyi (Veneridae), Macomona liliana (Tellinidae), Barbatia novaezealandiae (Arcidae), and Paphies australis (Mesodesmatidae), as well as farmed and wild populations of Haliotis iris (Haliotidae) in the North Island of New Zealand.

latest_report_detail.epidemiological_comments: From an epidemiological point of view, the Norwegian Food Safety Authority considers this ISA outbreak at Dønna to be a first occurrence. Infectious salmon anaemia (ISA) was present at another location 15 km away in July 2013 as well. The Norwegian Veterinary Institute uses genotyping to determine whether ISA outbreaks are an occurrence or a reoccurrence. The epidemiological survey relating to this ISA outbreak shows no genotypic association to the previous ISA outbreak at the other mentioned location. Therefore this event is reported as a first occurrence. The ISA cases seem to be two separate outbreaks without any epidemiological correlation, although both of them belong to the same administrative region, Nordland. The virus relating to the outbreak will be further characterized associated with the epidemiological studies.

latest_report_detail.epidemiological_comments: This event took place in August 2012 in 4 lakes among the several glacial lakes in Mercantour Park (Lac des Merveilles is one of the affected lakes, the largest of the four lakes). Agents from ONEMA (French National Agency for Water and Aquatic Environments) and from the Mercantour National Park observed this confined and mild phenomenon of mortalities during their round and took some samples. Investigations were aimed first at usual known pathogens (i.e. chytrid fungus) and tests were conducted for Ranavirus (known to be widespread in Europe). The presence of viruses of the family Ranavirus was detected on all the batches. Following this, sequencing was performed at the University of Savoie (CNRS) in December 2012 and was confirmed at the University of Ghent in Belgium in January 2013; the strain is identical to that isolated in newts in 2008 in Spain (common midwife toad ranavirus). In order to be able to establish a link between the causal agent (Ranavirus) and the disease (Ranavirosis), an experimental infection protocol was developed. These tests were conducted in 2013 in the Jura Veterinary Analysis Laboratory (LVD39) and showed in autumn 2013 that the isolated Ranavirus was pathogen and responsible for mortalities in common frogs observed in the lakes investigated in Mercantour Park. The LVD39 has sent this information in November 2013 to the OIE Reference Laboratory for amphibians, the Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organization (CSIRO), in Australia.

latest_report_detail.epidemiological_comments: Note 19/09/2024: This event was recreated in WAHIS due to the loss of data during migration for the update of the system. Infection with Perkinsus olseni was confirmed in New Zealand paua (Haliotis iris) from a single aquaculture facility. This is the first detection of this organism in New Zealand paua (Haliotis iris) and in farmed animals in New Zealand. Clinical signs (mantle retraction in shell) and gross pathology (nodules) were detected in farmed paua during harvest and prompted further laboratory investigation. Perkinsus was suspected after histopathological examination and the Ministry for Primary Industries was notified. New Zealand’s national laboratory received fixed and fresh samples from the affected farm and verified the presence of Perkinsus by histopathology, and confirmed P. olseni by conventional PCR (Audemard et al. 2004) and genetic sequencing. The Ministry for Primary Industries has conducted an epidemiological investigation of this event. Trace-forward and trace-back of movements from the farm were conducted. No elevated mortality in the affected farm has been observed. Perkinsus olseni is known to occur in wild populations of four species of bivalves from the Waitemata Harbour (Auckland) northwards. The affected farm is a semi-closed land-based system, and within the same region of New Zealand that P. olseni has previously been detected. The risk of P. olseni to wild populations of H. iris is unknown, but will be assessed during ongoing surveillance activities. Audemard C, Reece KS, Burreson EM. Real-time PCR for detection and quantification of the protistan parasite Perkinsus marinus in environmental waters. Appl Environ Microbiol. 2004 Nov;70(11):6611-8. doi: 10.1128/AEM.70.11.6611-6618.2004. PMID: 15528525; PMCID: PMC525192. Note: The amendment of the laboratory test (from real-time PCR test to conventional PCR test) was made by the request of the country on the 26th of March 2025.

latest_report_detail.epidemiological_comments: Movement controls in the form of an initial designation were applied to the individual farm sites, which prevented the onward movement of live oysters for farming or relay. Under the conditions of the designation, movements of Crassostrea gigas were permitted for direct human consumption; subject to hygiene regulations. In addition, the controls stipulated that disposal of dead Pacific oysters Crassostrea gigas of all stages must be by an approved method for disposal of Category 2 animal-by-product waste. The epidemiological investigation has been completed, the designations have been lifted and the incident has been closed. The mortalities occurred from late May and ceased in late July. On the 21st August the oysters were sampled by the Fish Health Inspectorate and showed no evidence of Mikrocytos mimicus or the presence of any listed diseases.

latest_report_detail.epidemiological_comments: - Through routine testing, Bonamia exitiosa infection was detected in Crassostrea virginica (Eastern American oyster) outside the known area of occurrence. The farmed species (C. virginica) were in open water. Mercenaria mercenaria seed of similar age held at the same site were laboratory tested negative for Bonamia infection. - Crassostrea virginica seed were hatchery-produced, tested negative for Bonamia infection, and then placed at nursery site when approximately one (1) month old. - The affected stock (C. virginica) showed no increased morbidity or mortality (sub-clinical). Prevalence determined by histology was approximately 23% and parasite was detected principally in gill tissues. Additional sampling and studies are to be conducted but no official action in relation to the infection with B. exitiosa event is planned at this time.

latest_report_detail.epidemiological_comments: - No elevated mortality in the affected stock was observed. - Improved resolution of Bonamia phylogeny allowed identification of Bonamia exitiosa infection in wild Ostrea stentina (= Ostreola equestris). The occurrence of B. exitiosa in wild O. stentina will be reported on future U.S. OIE six-monthly and annual reports. - The impact of B. exitiosa on commercial and wild populations of Crassostrea virginica is unknown. Current information indicates there is not widespread infection of C. virginica with B. exitiosa. - Follow-up sampling and laboratory testing of the B. exitiosa-affected hatchery indicates the prevalence of the infections was significantly reduced. No infections were heavy and no mortality was noted. It appears that the reductions in prevalence represent regression of infection rather than the disappearance through mortality. Additional sampling and studies are to be conducted but no official action in relation to the infection with B. exitiosa event is planned at this time. The B. exitiosa event is considered closed.

latest_report_detail.epidemiological_comments: Within a study conducted at the Federal University of Paraíba on the occurrence of diseases affecting native oysters Crassostrea spp., samples in oysters without clinical signs were taken in the estuary of the river Paraíba (Paraíba State - Brazil). The samples tested positive in an unofficial private laboratory. The official veterinary services of the Ministry of Fisheries and Aquaculture (MPA) were reported and new samples were taken and sent to an official laboratory of the MPA. No apparent loss of balance has been observed in the wild populations affected. The main area of commercial farms of bivalve molluscs of the country (State of Santa Catarina) is at about 2,700 km away from the outbreak. Note by the OIE Animal Health Information Department: Since this is the first time that infection with Perkinsus marinus is identified in the history of the country, the reason for notification as first occurrence applies to the country but the event is in fact circumscribed to a zone.

latest_report_detail.epidemiological_comments: Outbreak summary: • WSSV was detected during routine testing of broodstock shrimp as part of the Hawaii Department of Agriculture (HDOA) Shrimp Surveillance Certification Program (SSCP). • The HDOA placed a quarantine order on the movement of shrimp from the premises and a HDOA cleaning and disinfection (C&D) ‘premises clean-up plan’ was implemented. The premises remains under a quarantine order, and removal of the quarantine is contingent upon the successful completion of the ‘premises clean-up plan’. • Officials validated that no shrimp remained on the farm, including in the effluent pond. All ponds (except the unlined effluent pond), concrete tanks, raceways, and equipment used for shrimp production were drained and dried. • The premises owner has decided not to continue shrimp production. If the owner decides to continue shrimp production on the premises, the HDOA ‘premises clean-up plan’ requires additional C&D and surveillance prior to release of the quarantine. No more action, in relation to the WSSV event is planned at this time. The WSSV event is considered closed.

latest_report_detail.epidemiological_comments: In January 2009 an outbreak of ISA was confirmed in an Atlantic salmon fish farm in the South West Shetlands. Statutory controls were placed prohibiting any movements into and from the affected farm, as well as other farms in the Management Area. This totalled 13 farms in the local hydrographic area that were stocked with susceptible species and which required movement restrictions be put in place and surveillance to be undertaken. Stamping out was implemented on the affected farm. Further disease was then also confirmed in the surrounding Management Area that was also controlled through emergency stamping out. All the farms in the management area were then fallowed, prior to a restocking process in 10 of the farms with Atlantic salmon. All 10 of these farms were then under surveillance and sampled during the 18 month period of on-growing. No clinical signs of ISA or positive laboratory results for ISA were observed. Following this grow-out period, the 10 farms were harvested and left to fallow. The area is now considered to be ISA free, although movement restrictions will remain in place until the area is declared disease free of ISA under EU Community legislation in summer 2012.

latest_report_detail.epidemiological_comments: Epidemiology update as of 9 February 2012: • All five (5) affected ponds have been harvested, dried, cleaned & disinfected (C&D). This will be followed by testing of restocked shrimp for WSSV to validate C&D procedures. There are currently no clinical signs of WSSV in any ponds in the commodity/meat shrimp production facility, including previously affected ponds that were restocked. • The commodity/meat shrimp production facility has covered all individual grow out ponds with nets. • Repeat sampling and testing of the separate brood stock facilities will continue to be conducted – all testing to date is negative for WSSV. The WSSV event only involved the ‘meat’ shrimp production facility. The brood stock operation is a completely separate facility/premises and is not and has never been affected. No more action in relation to the WSSV event is planned at this time. The WSSV event is considered closed.

Statutory controls prohibiting the movement of live fish into and from the fishery were implemented, followed by a cull of the fish population. The fishery was then drained, disinfected, and remains dry and fallow. Statutory controls will remain in place until surveillance of other waters is completed in spring 2012.

latest_report_detail.epidemiological_comments: The Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry of New Zealand (MAF) investigated the syndrome of increased mortality in Pacific oysters (Crassostrea gigas). The cause of mortality in juvenile oysters is considered to be a combination of environmental factors and infection with OsHV-1. There has been no further report of mortality and the mortality event is considered resolved. The New Zealand virus sequence has the deletion considered characteristic of the micro variant strain. All of the samples tested by the MAFBNZ to date have been negative for relevant OIE-listed mollusc diseases including Marteilia refringens (type O), Bonamia species and Perkinsus species. Histopathology has not identified the presence of any Haplosporidian species.

latest_report_detail.epidemiological_comments: - Standard laboratory procedure pooled 5 animals in 1 reaction sample. - All stocks infected and non-infected were harvested and destroyed according to disinfection protocol laid down in Chapter 1.1.3, “Methods for disinfection of aquaculture establishments”, in the Manual of diagnostic tests for aquatic animals (2009). - Infected ponds were disinfected and treated. - No sales were permitted as all stocks were destroyed. - The intensity of the surveillance programme has been increased in all farms on a weekly basis and also in the hatcheries and wild stocks in order to prevent the transmission of diseases and also as a precautionary measure. - As a result of the intensive surveillance and biosecurity measures, no detection of diseases in the hatchery facilities. - The department of fisheries is continuing its surveillance on the farms, hatcheries, wet markets, importation and wild stocks. - All shrimp farms are sited in government gazetted areas, which allows the mitigation actions to be synchronized. - They are required to be registered and licensed by the Department of fisheries for the operation of the farm.

latest_report_detail.epidemiological_comments: This event was not associated with a visible die-off of finfish. This finding represents a new geographic location and a new species (brown bullhead, Ameiurus nebulosus). On 25 September 2010, sick fish were found in Hamilton harbour. The water temperature at the time of collection was 19 degrees Celsius. Seven adult brown bullheads were sent to Fisheries and Oceans Canada (DFO) for diagnostic work up. Another sample, 16 morbid adult brown bullheads, was submitted to DFO from the same location on 2 November 2010. On both submissions fish had deep ulcers on the head, base of fins and belly. Histological findings include severe mycotic ulcerative dermatitis and necrotizing granulomatous sub-acute myositis. Fungal structures were non-septate with occasional branching hyphae. No reproductive fungal structures were seen. Ulcerative lesions were also infected with bacteria.

latest_report_detail.epidemiological_comments: The New South Wales Department of Industry and Investment continues to investigate a syndrome of mortality in Pacific oysters (Crassostrea gigas), detected in the Georges River estuary and Botany Bay, New South Wales. Formal controls remain in place on the movement of oysters and oyster farming equipment from the Georges River and Botany Bay. There are also restrictions in place on the recreational take of oysters from the affected area. Laboratory testing found Ostreid herpesvirus 1 (OsHV-1) genetic material in association with the affected Pacific oysters; however, a causative role of this virus has not been established. A surveillance programme has been initiated to determine whether OsHV-1 (including OsHV-1 µ variant) is present in other Pacific oyster farming areas. The New South Wales Food Authority has advised that there is no evidence to suggest any food safety issues associated with infected oysters.

latest_report_detail.epidemiological_comments: Holiday makers at one of the fishing lodges within the Okavango delta reported some dead fish in the river to the Department of Wildlife and National Parks and also fishermen reported catching fish with ulcerative lesions (red dots) during the flood season in early August 2010. Subsequently, surveillance was initiated from 3 to 5 August setting up nets at Girigiri, Samochima and Tane Lagoons. Three species of fish (African catfish, silver catfish and African pike) were caught at Tane and Girigiri Lagoons while one species (African pike) was caught at Samochima Lagoon. The total number of fish caught at the three sites was 407 with 10 fish showing clinical lesions (6 at Tane, 3 at Girigiri and 1 at Samochima).

latest_report_detail.epidemiological_comments: This was a legal import of live ornamental goldfish which arrived in the United Kingdom and was cleared at Heathrow Border Inspection Post (GBLHR4). The consignment arrived with appropriate health certification from the Chinese authorities declaring freedom from SVC. A total of 35 boxes, containing 9,961 live fish arrived; on clearing through the Border Inspection Post, the consignment was held in secure quarantine by the importer to allow the animals to acclimatise after shipment. All fish in this consignment were maintained in this secure isolation until they were destroyed and the receiving site disinfected under the supervision of the competent authority in England, the Fish Health Inspectorate at the Centre for Environment, Fisheries & Aquaculture Science (CEFAS). The Chinese authorities have been informed of the SVC positive result in the imported fish.

latest_report_detail.epidemiological_comments: The OIE Reference Laboratory in Tucson (Arizona, United States) confirmed the diagnosis of infectious myonecrosis. There were no clinical signs or deaths related to this event. After the results from the Federal University Laboratory of Santa Catarina (Brazil) were received, all ponds with positive samples for the disease were depopulated. The animals were slaughtered and destroyed by burning on 14 February 2008. Cleaning and disinfection of the ponds were carried out and water was directed towards the effluent treatment system and an outlet. A 30-day sanitation period was established. Surveillance went on and no other outbreak was observed. The event is considered resolved.

latest_report_detail.epidemiological_comments: Based on the findings below, the French authorities have authorized the French mollusc culture areas to return to their normal activities as from 12 September 2008. The situation has now returned to normal. 1/Background Since May 2008, French farmers observed a significant mortality in oysters throughout the French coastline, at all stages of production, from spats to animals aged 18-24 months. Appropriate management measures were taken to contain these deaths and prevent the spread. This notice aims to show the evolution of this event and of the information gathered about it. 2/Measures implemented a) Looking for the possible reasons for this mortality The monitoring committee for these mortalities meets regularly to consolidate the local information available on the topic. The most likely reason to explain the event occurred this summer is the presence of pathogenic agents associated with environmental and climatic factors and animal management practices. The experimental study on resowing in a natural environment which began in early August in collaboration with the national reference laboratory for shellfish pathology, State services and professionals, has shown at successive counts a significant decrease in percentage of dead animals between the two counts. The synthesis of national records on deaths at sea or in hatcheries and imports has led to define the preconditions for trade and exports of flat oyster spats from France. To better know and understand this event, the Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries has required a thorough epidemiological investigation which focuses on all segments of production and on shipments and imports. The reason for this event should become clearer in a few months. b) Ensuring the protection of consumers’ health The health monitoring set up within the health and agriculture services have permitted to verify that no impact on consumers’ health has been observed. c) Avoiding the spread Following the counting of dead animals in the frame of the test protocol on resowing and in agreement with the recommendation of the AFSSA (French Agency for Food Safety) on 12 September 2008, the immersion of spats has gradually been permitted from 12 September (Channel and Atlantic) to 24 September (Mediterranean). In its recommendation on 25 September 2008, the AFSSA states that the risk of transmission to other production areas in case of immersion of animals originating from France in waters of another country may not be effective if the following conditions are met: * Strict compliance with conditions required in the certificate; * Checking previously the health situation of production facilities, which should be considered satisfactory; * Animals to be exported should be found by physical inspection in good health and with no abnormal mortality observed. Health certificates accompanying the flat oyster spats traded or exported from French farms will be established based on these requirements, checked before signing any certificate. 3/Conclusion The monitoring of the animals in the French mollusc culture areas carried out since this summer shows that this mortality event declared in a concurrent and significant manner throughout the French coastline is now finished. The situation is now returned to normal. Based on these findings, the French authorities have authorized the French mollusc culture areas to return to their normal activities as from 12 September 2008. In addition, following the results observed on restart of activities and based on the recommendation of the AFSSA on 25 September 2008, trade and exports of flat oyster spats are authorized, subject to verification by the control services of certain conditions concerning the farm of origin and the health status of the batch exported. An epidemiological investigation is underway to provide further information that could help explain this event.

normalized_disease_name: Infection with white spot syndrome virus

latest_report_detail.epidemiological_comments: Summary of expanded surveillance testing in May and June 2007: • 74 of the 111 farm ponds tested were positive for White Spot Syndrome Virus (WSSV) on PCR tests conducted at the Louisiana Animal Diagnostic Laboratory. • Ponds located in 13 of the 18 Parishes from which samples were collected had at least one positive pond disclosed. • Four samples out of thirteen collected from the Atchafalaya Basin were positive for WSSV. • Of the ponds testing positive for WSSV (74), only 13.5% (10/74) displayed clinical signs and of these only 6.7% (5/74) displayed a significant mortality. Louisiana consumes up to 99% of the crawfish it produces. In consideration of the expanded surveillance testing and the in-state consumption of produced crawfish, Louisiana has declared that WSSV in Louisiana crawfish is endemic. Any further testing will be conducted for the purpose of managing the disease, currently zoned to the State of Louisiana.

latest_report_detail.epidemiological_comments: The Taura syndrome virus (TSV) detection event in Oahu, Hawaii was limited to one premises. • All enhanced surveillance activities, and epidemiological investigations have been completed. No more positive cases. Event Summary: • Sub-clinical Taura syndrome virus outbreak confirmed April 18, 2007 on routine testing as part of the Hawaii Aquaculture Development Program, which certifies farms as pathogen-free. The virus was identified at the shrimp farm in an above-ground concrete pond. • The two retention ponds from which positive confirmatory samples had been collected were drained, depopulated, cleaned and disinfected (C&D) according to regulatory guidance. • The outdoor raceways where the original suspect positive samples were located have been cleaned and disinfected and remained empty for 30 days after all shrimp were removed. • Test results received May 31, 2007 indicated: o Hatchery remained negative o Two outdoor raceways yielded positive test results for TSV • The ponds and raceways were emptied of water and shrimp. All retention ponds and raceways have been filled in/ knocked down or remain dry and empty. • The owner plans on utilizing only tanks within the hatchery, which have been tested and all tests have yielded negative results for TSV. o The only shrimp on the premises are the brood stock in the hatchery • The Hawaii Department of Agriculture (HDOA) in cooperation with the owner have implemented a plan for raising shrimp in the hatchery, including stocking densities, tank location, and testing numbers and dates. The TSV event is considered closed.

reason_for_notification: First occurrence in a zone or a compartment

raw_fields.reason: First occurrence in a zone or a compartment

latest_report_detail.epidemiological_comments: The site encompasses a small area of the sea bed, exposed only at low spring tide, on which post graded Ostrea edulis, too small for market, have been relaid. The site is considered as fallow, following inspection on 16 June 2006 when 31 Ostrea edulis were removed and tested. On the first low water spring tide, the area is to be raked and searched for any remaining oysters. In addition, a diver is to search sublittorally for the presence of any which may have migrated from the designated area. Anecdotal evidence suggests no wild populations of native oysters in the loch. However, investigations will be made to confirm this. If any are found they will be tested for Bonamia.

latest_report_detail.reason_for_notification: Listed disease occurring in a new host species
latest_report_detail.epidemiological_comments: Multiple occurrence of the disease have been confirmed in the Great Lakes affecting wild fish including multiple new species. Diagnostics have been conducted by: •New York: Cornell University, Dr. Paul Bowser using cell culture (EPC, BF2 cells) and confirmation using PCR by the Western Fisheries Research Center, Dr. Jim Winton. •Michigan: Michigan State University, Dr. Mohammed Faisal using cell culture and confirmation by PCR. •Ohio: US Fish and Wildlife – La Crosse Fish Health Center, culture using EPC, CHSE-214 and BF2 and confirmation using PCR by the Western Fisheries Research Center, Dr. Jim Winton. Depending on the species affected, die-offs have ranged from a few fish (large muskellunge) to several thousand. Many of these species of fish are currently not listed in the Aquatic Animal Health Code as being susceptible to VHS. The event is continuing and unlikely to be resolved because it affects wild fish. No eradication will be done, and consequently, it is considered endemic in wildlife in this zone. Note (04/05/2023): In 2005, the WAHIS system did not allow to distinguish between domestic and wild species. Due to subsequent evolutions of the system, the species initially listed in this report were automatically labelled as domestic, whereas they were actually wild species, as indicated in the epidemiological comments. For this reason, the species were amended to reflect the reality of the situation.
outbreaks: 10508 - ST. LAWRENCE RIVER AND LAKE ONTARIO (IRONDIQUOIT BAY)

latest_report_detail.epidemiological_comments: The affected fish were traced to a trial batch of 30 fish imported from a new source in Malaysia. The entire batch was submitted to the laboratory for PCR testing for koi herpesvirus. Although the imported fish were isolated, a follow-up investigation was conducted at the affected importer premises. All koi carp at the importer’s premises were sampled for laboratory testing. The results of the PCR testing were negative. Quarantine on the movement of koi carp was imposed on the affected importer. Based on official import data, all fish importers that imported koi carp from Malaysia after August 2005 were traced. These importers were inspected and koi carp were collected for PCR testing. All the samples from these importers tested negative. Singapore remains free from koi herpesvirus infection.
